new.title: Origin of the angular momentum of filaments in the local Universe
new.summary: Velocity gradients compatible with rotation have been reported across certain nearby cosmic filaments. We show that rotational momentum might be generated in filaments in the local Universe in the presence of a cosmological constant (local dark energy) based on the theorem stating the general function for the equivalence of the gravitational field of a sphere and that of a point mass. We investigated how the cosmological constant modifies the finite-time acquisition and retention of angular momentum in an open filamentary core. Although its isotropic force exerts no direct axial torque, rotational motion can be seeded by tidal interactions with surrounding matter and incoming streams. Early tidal torques establish an imbalance in axial angular momentum, while the subsequent orbit crossing amplifies the resulting rotation, and ultimately, the cosmological constant is able to modify tidal-mode growth and finite-time angular momentum delivery.

new.title: What the X-ray Emission from Young Supernovae Can Tell Us About Their Progenitors
new.summary: We discuss constraints that the X-ray emission from supernovae can place on their progenitor stars. Since almost all X-ray supernovae arise from massive stars, we concentrate on implications for massive stars. These stars lose mass throughout their lifetime in the form of stellar winds. X-ray emission can be used to gauge the wind properties, especially the mass-loss rates, via various techniques. The abundance of various elements formed by nucleosynthesis within the stars, and released in the stellar explosion, can be estimated from X-ray spectra. In many cases, a combination of X-ray light curves and spectra can allow us to extricate the structure and morphology of the surrounding medium formed by pre-supernova mass loss into which the SN shock is expanding.

The inclusion of the stellar photons results in the formation of a dense photo-ionized HII region interior to the shell. Going outwards in radius from the central star, the various regions are (1) the freely expanding wind, (2) the shocked wind, (3) the photo-ionized (HII) region, (4) the dense swept-up shell (equatorial ring) and (5) the red-supergiant wind from the previous epoch. Details of the simulation and the modeling technique are described in Dwarkadas (2022) .

new.title: Jet energetics and remnant magnetism in short gamma-ray bursts from binary neutron-star mergers: A statistical study via broadband afterglow modeling
new.summary: Short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) are believed to originate from compact binary mergers, particularly binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, providing a probe of jet energetics and merger remnants. We compile broadband afterglow observations of 40 sGRBs and perform forward-shock modeling with off-axis Gaussian jets, excluding data potentially affected by additional energy injection. We derive distributions of beaming-corrected jet kinetic energy $E_k$ and radiative efficiency $\eta_\gamma$, and combine these with binary population synthesis and numerical simulations to infer remnant black hole (BH) magnetic fields assuming the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) jet-launching mechanism. For the 15 strictly constrained bursts, we find a median $E_k\simeq3.8\times10^{49}$ erg and $\eta_\gamma\simeq0.35$, with respective 68% intervals of $[5.1\times10^{48},1.9\times10^{50}]$ erg and [0.09, 0.79]. The inferred magnetic field supplied by the accretion disk and threading the BH horizon is approximately $7\times10^{15}$ G, with a 68% credible interval of $[2.3\times10^{15},2.4\times10^{16}]$ G, depending slightly on the neutron star equation of state. The full sample yields a higher median field of approximately $2\times10^{16}$ G, with the high-energy and high-field tails predominantly contributed by less well-constrained bursts. These results provide statistical constraints on sGRB jet energetics and suggest characteristic BH magnetic fields of order $10^{16}$ G. Comparison with pre-merger neutron star magnetic fields indicates a characteristic amplification factor of $\eta_B\sim10^3$, providing an observational constraint on magnetic field amplification during BNS mergers and subsequent BH formation.

new.title: Machine-Learning Reconstruction of Intergalactic Medium Column-Density Maps from Observed Ly$α$ Emission Cubes
new.summary: Understanding the large-scale structure of the intergalactic medium (IGM) is essential for studying galaxy evolution, particularly at $z \sim 2$--$6$, when cold filaments in the cosmic web are considered a primary mechanism for fueling galaxy growth. At these redshifts, Ly$\alpha$ emission shifts into the optical regime and serves as the primary tracer of diffuse IGM for ground-based integral field units (IFUs). However, detections remain limited by low signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) and the complexities of resonant scattering. We present a proof-of-concept machine-learning framework to reconstruct IGM gas column-density maps from noisy Ly$\alpha$ IFU emission cubes. Using Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) observations of $z \sim 2.3$ protoclusters as a case study, we train a custom convolutional neural network (CNN), the Column Density Estimator (CDE), on a simulated dataset combining IllustrisTNG100 with simplified radiative-transfer calculations and an approximate treatment of KCWI noise. The CDE successfully reconstructs broad filamentary structures in the simulated test set under these adopted assumptions. Applied to observed KCWI data, the CDE predicts gas column-density maps containing filamentary structures extending over $\gtrsim 40''$ ($\sim 1$ comoving Mpc), consistent with an IGM interpretation. The observed reconstructions remain conditional on the adopted models. These results illustrate the potential of the CDE framework for connecting diffuse Ly$\alpha$ observations with simulations of the IGM.

new.title: C$_2$ Swan, CH and CN emission, surface temperature and luminous efficiency of the Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule from ground-based spectroscopy
new.summary: The Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule entered the atmosphere over South Australia on 5 December 2020 at 12 km/s. A slitless spectral video, taken from the ground with a hand-tracked consumer camera, shows the capsule alone from 80 to 49 km. In the first ten seconds of heating the shock layer emits the CN violet system, the CH A-X band and the C$_2$ Swan bands, the latter for the first time in remote observations of a capsule entry. C$_2$ ($T_{\rm rot}\approx9200$ K, $T_{\rm vib}\approx7800$ K) and CN (about 7000 K) are far hotter than the surface. C$_2$ and CH disappear while the heat flux is still rising and CN persists, which we relate to the early pyrolysis of the carbon-phenolic ablator and to the changing boundary-layer chemistry. The colour temperature of the heat shield rises from 2720 to 3080 K, in agreement with airborne results. The radiated energy is one to two orders of magnitude below that of natural fireballs, because the light comes from the hot surface rather than from ablation vapour. A faint persistent train lights up about 1 s after the passage and fades within a few seconds, probably chemiluminescence in the cooling wake.

new.title: 3D radiative transfer of K-series lines of He-like ions with SKIRT
new.summary: High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy with XRISM has resolved line profiles of highly ionised ions, including P Cygni profiles, in many systems containing compact objects. To interpret these line profiles, forward modelling with three-dimensional radiative transfer (3D RT) calculations including the relevant ionic processes is required. Following our previous work on the Lyman-series lines of H-like ions, we present the implementation of the K-series lines of He-like ions with Z = 2-30 in the open-source Monte Carlo RT code SKIRT, providing a numerical tool for interpreting highresolution X-ray spectra of photoionised plasmas. Building upon the framework developed for H-like ions, we incorporate the resonance scattering (RS) and radiative recombination (RR) channels. We also implement the inner-shell ionisation (II) channel of Li-like ions for the production of He-like lines. We resolve fine-structure levels and account for level populations, frequency redistribution, phase function, and linear polarisation through transition-specific Mueller matrices. The implementation reproduces the expected RT effects in He-like lines. The Fe xxv w and y lines, dominated by the RS channel, develop optically thick line-profile distortions and P Cygni profiles in an outflowing plasma, whereas the x and z lines, dominated by the RR and II channels, do not exhibit such behaviour. The line intensities from the RS and RR channels agree well with Cloudy. The II channel further enhances the z line, which is not yet included in Cloudy. The linear polarisation calculations reproduce the analytical and experimental angular dependence of resonance scattering on a line-by-line basis. This extension to He-like lines, together with our previous implementation of H-like lines, enables 3D RT modelling of the major X-ray lines, providing a tool for constraining gas kinematics around compact objects observed with XRISM.

new.title: Galaxy Clustering Topology in Observations and Cosmological Simulations
new.summary: We present a genus topology analysis of the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data (SDSS), comparing the observed topology with mock galaxy samples from the Horizon Run 4 (HR4) $N$-body simulation and four cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. We construct nine volume-limited samples and measure their genus curves at Gaussian smoothing scales of $4$--$12~h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$. Overall, the modern galaxy models reproduce the observed genus statistics substantially better than the HGC, HOD, and SAM models examined by Choi et al. (2010). Among the models considered here, the HR4 Most-Bound-Halo Particle galaxy-assignment model shows somewhat better overall agreement with the SDSS topology than IllustrisTNG300 and FLAMINGO. The observed scale dependences of the genus shift parameter $\Delta\nu_f$ and void abundance parameter $A_V$ are somewhat steeper than those predicted by the simulations, but their joint discrepancy from HR4 is not statistically significant. The smaller-volume TNG100 and EAGLE realizations show significant excesses in $A_C$, at $4.5\sigma$ and $7.0\sigma$, respectively, relative to the observational uncertainties. When the expected cosmic variance of the simulations is taken into account, they do not necessarily indicate failures of the galaxy-formation prescriptions, but they caution that individual small-volume realizations may not be representative of the observed galaxy topology. Overall, modern galaxy formation models reproduce the observed topology substantially better than earlier models, while residual differences remain that can be tested more precisely with denser future surveys.

new.title: B-fields And Dust in InterstelLar FiLAments Using Dust POLarization (BALLAD-POL): V. Magnetic Fields and Grain Alignment Mechanisms in Serpens Main Using JCMT/POL-2 Polarization
new.summary: We investigate magnetic fields ($B$-field) and grain alignment mechanisms in Serpens Main using 850 $\mu$m dust polarization observations from JCMT/POL-2. We derive a map of $B$-field strength and calculate the mass-to-flux ratio and Alfvénic Mach number, suggesting the subdominance of $B$-fields over gravity but their dominance over turbulence. Fitting the Ricean mean model to the nondebiased polarization fraction ($P$) as a function of emission intensity ($I$) yields a slope $\alpha = 0.68\pm0.01$, revealing depolarization. To understand its origins, we examine the dependence of $P$ on gas column density ($N({\rm H}_{2})$), dust temperature ($T_{\rm d}$), and polarization angle dispersion function ($S$). We find no correlation between $P$ and $S$, whereas for $P\times S$, an observational proxy for alignment efficiency decreases with increasing $N({\rm H}_{2})$. This suggests that $B$-field tangling is not the primary cause of depolarization and instead points to reduced grain alignment in denser regions. To test this interpretation within radiative torque (RAT) alignment theory, we calculate the minimum size of aligned grains ($a_{\rm align}$) and magnetic relaxation strength ($\delta_{\rm mag,sp}$) using $N({\rm H}_{2})$, $T_{\rm d}$, and our estimated $B$-field map. We find that both $P$ and $P \times S$ decrease with increasing $a_{\rm align}$, supporting reduced grain alignment as the main cause of depolarization in Serpens Main. However, neither $P$ nor $P \times S$ shows a correlation with $\delta_{\rm mag,sp}$, suggesting that enhanced grain alignment due to magnetic relaxation is insufficient to compensate for the reduced alignment associated with increasing $a_{\rm align}$ toward denser regions.

new.title: Stellar Loci XI: Identifications and Parameter Determinations of Binary Stars by multi-band photometry
new.summary: Large photometric surveys contain numerous unresolved binaries, but identifying them and measuring component properties remains challenging. We present a 65-band UV-to-IR SED-fitting framework to identify unresolved main-sequence binaries and infer their parameters. Photometry combines synthetic miniJPAS magnitudes from corrected Gaia DR3 XP spectra with 2MASS and WISE measurements. Using LAMOST-calibrated, metallicity-dependent stellar loci and a dwarf-star color-absolute-magnitude relation, we construct forward models for single stars and unresolved binaries. We fit both model families to each SED with MCMC, using Gaia distances as Hertzsprung-Russell-diagram constraints to infer metallicity, reddening, and component photometric parameters. Component masses and mass ratios are derived from PARSEC models. Simulations show the method robustly recovers binary parameters. Tests on a LAMOST comparison sample indicate sensitivity to binaries with $q\gtrsim0.4$; the preferred model reproduces spectroscopic metallicities with 0.11 dex scatter, while inferred reddenings agree with external extinction maps with $\sim0.02$ mag scatter. Comparison with an external Gaia XP-based binary catalog shows broadly consistent binary classifications for common sources. Our metallicities more closely follow the LAMOST spectroscopic scale, and mass-ratio estimates in the intermediate-$q$ regime better trace expected $\Delta$-HRD offsets. Tests using M67 members support internal consistency of inferred parameters. For quality-selected Gaia non-single-star binaries, primary-mass estimates agree with Gaia NSS values with 0.071 $M_\odot$ residual scatter; in cases with larger discrepancies, further tests indicate that secondary-mass and mass-ratio estimates are more reliable than the Gaia NSS values. The method scales to large photometric samples, enabling population studies and analyses of individual systems.

new.title: Minimal vacuum histories beyond $Λ$CDM: model comparison within VCDM
new.summary: Recent cosmological observations motivate alternatives to $\Lambda$CDM with evolving dark energy. We compare three such models, each introducing one additional cosmological parameter: F42, with equation of state $w(a)=w_0/\sqrt{a}$, and two smooth sign-changing effective dark-energy profiles, Ag and Qui. All models are implemented within VCDM, which determines the background and linear perturbations without introducing an additional propagating gravitational degree of freedom. We use CMB observations from SPT, Planck, and ACT, combined with DESI DR2 distance measurements, with and without the DESY5 Dovekie supernova sample. All three alternatives improve the best-fit likelihood relative to $\Lambda$CDM. When supernovae are included, the Akaike information criterion favors F42, while Ag and Qui remain nearly indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM on this criterion. The Bayesian evidence, however, does not establish a robust preference among the three alternatives. Our results show that improved fits to current observations can arise from physically different dark-energy histories, motivating complementary measurements of expansion and structure growth to distinguish them.

new.title: EP250226a: A fast X-ray transient associated with GRB 250226A and its multiwavelength afterglow properties
new.summary: Recent advances in fast X-ray transient studies have been driven by the wide-field, sensitive soft X-ray monitoring capabilities of the Einstein Probe (EP), enabling the prompt detection and localization of previously underexplored events. EP observations offer new opportunities to investigate the origins, emission mechanisms, and population properties of newly discovered fast X-ray transients. We present multiwavelength observations of EP250226a, an extragalactic fast X-ray transient associated with GRB 250226A. We jointly analyze the prompt emission from soft X-rays to gamma rays and the X-ray afterglow spectra. We collect optical photometric data, perform empirical and afterglow model-based analyses, and present optical-to-infrared spectroscopy, measuring the equivalent widths of absorption lines. The spectroscopic redshift is $z = 3.314$, and the isotropic-equivalent gamma-ray energy is $E_\mathrm{iso}\simeq7.32\times10^{53}$ erg. Its location in the Amati diagram is consistent with a massive-star core-collapse origin (Type II GRB). The fluence ratio $\rm{S}(25-50\,\rm{keV})/\rm{S}(50-100\,\rm{keV})=0.57\pm0.06$ supports its classification as a classical GRB. The X-ray and optical afterglows show achromatic behavior. Among the models considered, a top-hat jet propagating into a uniform interstellar medium best describes the multiwavelength afterglow. This model suggests a highly collimated, nearly on-axis jet, with an isotropic-equivalent kinetic energy of $E_\mathrm{k,iso}\simeq4.07\times10^{55}$ erg, a gamma-ray radiative efficiency of $\eta_{\gamma}\simeq 1.77\%$, and a low magnetic-field energy fraction of $\log \epsilon_\mathrm{B,FS} \simeq -6.52$. EP250226a exhibits typical long-duration GRB properties, with the first soft X-ray peak coinciding with the gamma-ray prompt emission, while the soft X-ray emission lasts significantly longer than the gamma-ray emission.

new.title: Polarized transport in a Thomson slab: Stokes recursion, asymptotic eigenmodes, and Comptonization applications
new.summary: We develop a scattering-order-resolved Stokes-vector recursion for axisymmetric polarized transport in a finite plane-parallel Thomson slab. The post-scattering radiation field closes exactly within two depth-dependent coefficients, yielding escape probabilities, angular distributions and linear polarization while conserving photon number. At high scattering orders, the principal eigenmode of the weighted self-adjoint transport operator controls the escape statistics, and the normalized angular distribution and polarization become independent of the seed source. The subdominant spectrum quantifies convergence, with the characteristic scattering order scaling as the square of the optical depth in thick slabs. We derive logarithmic corrections to the thin-slab complete-polarization limit away from the slab normal, together with a finite-optical-depth Galerkin approximation. In optically thick slabs, matching bulk diffusion to a polarized Milne surface layer yields finite-thickness corrections to the Chandrasekhar solution. We provide compact formulae for the principal and leading subdominant eigenvalues and the asymptotic angular and polarization distributions across both regimes. Combining the recursion with an angle-averaged thermal-Compton redistribution kernel gives approximate energy-resolved Stokes spectra. Comparisons with full polarized Compton calculations show that this separable reconstruction is most reliable for cool, optically thick media. Applied to the non-dipping observations of neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary system 4U 1624-49, the model provides acceptable joint fits to the broadband intensity and IXPE Stokes spectra, showing that an extended corona overlying the accretion disc can account for the observed X-ray polarization.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). The PHZ processing function for the physical properties of galaxies
new.summary: Euclid is a European Space Agency mission mapping the extragalactic sky, aiming to provide the most-accurate 3D view of the Universe at optical and near-infrared wavelengths, by measuring the photometric redshifts of billions of galaxies. Within the Euclid Consortium, this task is executed by the PHZ Organisation Unit. PHZ takes as input the multi-wavelength photometry of Euclid and ground-based data, and returns as output the source classification, photometric redshifts for the Euclid core science (i.e., cosmology), and photometric redshifts plus physical parameters and absolute magnitudes for non-cosmological science. As part of the first Euclid Data Release (DR1), we describe the details of the DR1 pipeline for non-cosmological science, along with the released data products, and their validation. The non-cosmological science data products are obtained with NNPZ, a nearest-neighbour algorithm developed within PHZ that infers the properties of each target galaxy from its closest matches, in colour-magnitude space, within a reference sample of galaxies with known redshifts and physical parameters. We built this reference sample from Euclid observations of COSMOS, one of the Euclid Auxiliary Fields, labelling each galaxy with redshifts and physical parameters derived from the COSMOS2020 multi-wavelength photometry, consistently with the Euclid core-science results. Combined with the adjustments and priors required to generalise the results across the entire extragalactic sky, this approach yields high-quality and internally consistent data products. We tested the performance using both internal metrics and comparisons to ancillary data sets (e.g., COSMOS2020, 3D-HST, and DESI) and scaling relations (e.g., the star-forming main sequence); the results are in line with expectations and pre-DR1 simulations for both the Euclid Wide Survey and Euclid Deep Fields.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). An overview of the Science Ground Segment architecture and operations
new.summary: The Euclid mission is designed to address fundamental questions on the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the extragalactic sky with a wide-area survey complemented by targeted deep observations. The required scientific performance places stringent demands on the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), which transforms raw telemetry into calibrated, validated, and scientifically exploitable products. The SGS is a distributed system comprising the Euclid Science Operations Centre, the Science Data Centres, Instrument Operation Teams, and supporting Organisation Units, within a common architectural and procedural framework. This paper presents the SGS as implemented for Data Release 1 (DR1), describing its organisation, architecture, processing functions, and operational model. We outline the main components of the SGS common infrastructure. A key element is the Euclid Archive System (EAS), the central metadata repository based on a common data model. It comprises a Distributed Storage System, providing scalable storage of data files across the Science Data Centres; a Data Processing System used by the pipelines to register and access files and their lineage; and a Science Archive, distributing validated data products. Processing is coordinated by a common orchestration framework based on the Infrastructure Abstraction Layer, providing workflow management and resource abstraction of distributed compute clusters. Software development, integration, and deployment are supported by the Common Development Environment. We describe daily operations, calibration, and quality control, followed by the DR1 production campaign, including processing flows, validation strategy, and computational and data volumes. This infrastructure enabled Euclid DR1, involving 35 million jobs across nine Science Data Centres and 6.7 million core-hours, demonstrating robustness and scalability of the SGS.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). NIR astrometric calibration
new.summary: This paper presents the methodology and results of the astrometric calibration applied to the Euclid Near-Infrared (NIR) images in the Euclid Data Release 1, focusing on the techniques used to model and correct instrumental distortions, as well as the assessment of calibration quality. This work details the calibration pipeline, including quality control tests, and the evaluation of astrometric residuals against the Gaia DR3 catalogue and internal consistency metrics based on data encompassing more than one year of Euclid operation: the achieved accuracy is 30 mas for 97% of the total area, thus exceeding the requirements for Data Release 1. For the remaining 3%, accuracy declines due to a persistence correction issue: a method to correct the issue is presented. Furthermore, we discuss the stability of the solution over time, its dependence on source properties and instrument configuration, and outline the improvements planned for future Euclid data releases to enhance the astrometric calibration accuracy and efficiency.

new.title: The Black Hole Mass of the Sunflower Galaxy NGC 5055: Direct Measurement via Stellar Kinematics with Keck/OSIRIS Laser Guide Star Adaptive Optics
new.summary: We present the first stellar-dynamical supermassive black hole mass measurement in the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 5055 (M63) using near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with Keck/OSIRIS assisted by the laser guide star adaptive optics system. The observations deliver two-dimensional stellar kinematics extracted from the CO bandhead absorption features via pPXF at an angular resolution of $0.045''$. The stellar velocity dispersion rises steeply from $\sim90~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$ at $r\sim1''$ to a central peak of $\sim135~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$, kinematically tracing the gravitational influence of a central mass concentration. Modeling these kinematics with an ensemble of four JAM models, spanning cylindrical and spherical velocity-ellipsoid alignments and two independent MGE decompositions of archival HST imaging, yields a black hole mass of $M_{\rm BH}=4.56^{+1.73}_{-1.82}\times10^6~{\rm M_\odot}$. The stellar orbits are consistent with near-isotropy ($\beta\approx0$), typical of rotating late-type galaxies. NGC 5055 emerges as a remarkable local analogue to the Milky Way in terms of its black hole, nuclear star cluster, and total stellar mass. The surface brightness profile of NGC 5055 shows no evidence for a classical bulge; if confirmed bulgeless, NGC 5055 would join the rare class of spirals with a direct dynamical $M_{\rm BH}$ determination in the absence of a bulge, a regime currently populated by only a handful of galaxies including NGC 2748 and NGC 4395. This measurement provides a new anchor for black hole scaling relations in late-type galaxies at the low-mass end of the black hole mass spectrum.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) - NISP-P point-spread function modelling pipelines
new.summary: The images collected in photometric mode by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) instrument of the Euclid satellite are used to model the point-spread function (PSF) of a selection of sources detected in single and combined frames. We used Q1 and DR1 data to improve the development of the PSF module of the near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) and to refine the models currently provided. We explored a few methods normally used to evaluate the quality of the derived models and discuss possible variations related to the position of the sources in the focal plane and to the wavelength and time of the observations. The procedure of fitting the PSF profile, compared to other methods used for flux estimation, such as aperture photometry, indicates that updated models are better than those provided by Q1 images. The current results are in agreement with several key requirements defined for the mission, but there is still room for further improvements, which we plan to investigate and implement in future releases.

new.title: Euclid: Data Release 1 (DR1) - First NISP emission-line maps: Methodology, validation, and applications to galaxy evolution
new.summary: We demonstrate the capability of the slitless spectroscopic mode of the Euclid Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) to produce emission-line maps analogous to narrow-band images with user-defined central wavelengths. We present the first such maps of galaxies at $0.4 < z < 0.9$, constructed from blue-grism exposures obtained during the Euclid performance-verification observations of the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field in November 2023. We demonstrate the use of these maps for identifying star-forming clumps, measuring radial star-formation profiles, detecting projected internal velocity gradients, deblending the H$\alpha$--[N II] complex, and assessing spectroscopic redshift measurements. As a first statistical application, we reconstruct the galaxy mass--metallicity relation for 885 galaxies observed with the blue grism at $0.4 < z < 0.9$ by deblending the H$\alpha$--[N II] complex in the emission-line maps, and measure stacked H$\alpha$ radial profiles for 2634 galaxies over the same redshift range. The mass--metallicity relation is consistent with that obtained from the Euclid 1D spectroscopic measurements, demonstrating overall agreement between the two deblending approaches. The recovered H$\alpha$ radial profiles broadly follow the $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ stellar continuum but remain modestly more extended after matching the $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ images to the H$\alpha$ PSF, consistent with previous results in the literature. Across the four $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ size bins, we measure a mean $R_{50,\mathrm{H}\alpha}/R_{50,Y_{\mathrm{E}}}=1.15$.

new.title: Euclid First Data Release 1 (DR1) - Data release overview
new.summary: This paper describes the contents of the Euclid First Data Release (DR1), together with the set of papers that document the data-processing and the data products. DR1 consists of two parts: first `DR1-Foundation', releasing images, spectra, and catalogues in November 2026. Second, the shear measurements and the `Level~3' products required for cosmological analyses will be added in June 2027 to complete the full DR1. This data set contains around a billion catalogued objects, mainly from the Euclid Wide Survey (1975\,deg$^2$) and the Euclid Deep Fields (77\,deg$^2$)

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Colouring Euclid with external ground-based imaging data
new.summary: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10\sigma$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. (Abridged)

new.title: Self-Organizing Maps for the Exploration and Classification of X-Ray Sources in the Chandra Source Catalog
new.summary: In this work, we apply Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to the Chandra Source Catalog (CSC) to investigate the distribution of observation-level detections in the feature space defined by their spectral and variability properties. SOMs are neural-network-based models that project points in high-dimensional space onto a two-dimensional latent space while preserving their local topological structure. From CSC 2.1.1 we extract a sample of 36,904 ACIS-only, observation-level, high statistical significance detections, belonging to 17,927 unique sources. Among these detections, 25,192 (10,078 sources) are associated with a label from SIMBAD via a 1" cross-match that provides information about their astrophysical nature. Training a 40x40 hexagonal SOM reveals structured regions in the U-Matrix and activation response map, and feature-projection maps trace coherent patterns in spectral shape and variability. Overlaying SIMBAD classes shows that labeled populations occupy distinct, partially adjacent regions of the map and that generic categories can be interpreted via their SOM locations. We then retrain the SOM for classification using a source-grouped train/validation/test split and introduce SOMClassifier. When applied to 11,712 detections without SIMBAD labels, it assigns valid (non-abstained) labels to 6,225 detections (coverage ~53%). Furthermore, we release the trained models and visualization/classification workflows through a public web application built on the most up-to-date CSC release.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Calibration strategy and observations
new.summary: This paper reviews how Euclid's top-level calibration requirements were translated into a calibration plan, how this plan is implemented and maintained during the survey, and how it performs in the current DR1 release. We show that DR1 already meets or exceeds most end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration requirements. The construction of spectroscopically complete and pure samples relies on ongoing data acquisition for the Euclid Deep Survey, while point-spread-function modelling and shear calibration are still converging to their stringent accuracy requirements. With all DR1 data reprocessed with the DR1 pipeline configuration, more subtle effects have been detected and characterised, and correction strategies have been developed for DR2. These include improved absolute flux calibration, astrometry, charge-persistence correction, shutter effects, wavelength calibration, and spectrophotometric corrections for water-ice contamination. Finally, synthetic photometric transformations between Euclid and each of Roman, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope, are presented.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Spacecraft performance in the L2 environment
new.summary: The Euclid mission was designed around the need for thermo-optical and mechanical stability, stray-light suppression, low outgassing, and precise guiding. After three years in space, a wealth of data is available to assess the performance in these areas. We review the L2 halo-orbit design and consumables budget. Solar stray-light gradually increases by 14\% per year and is consistent with meteoroid puncturing, but remains low overall. Data loss from high solar activity has declined notably since the maximum of the 25th Solar cycle passed. The thermodynamical response of the optical elements to a thermal step impulse follows sigmoidal growth curves, entering the asymptotic equilibration regime after 21--46 hours. Water-ice contamination has affected data from both instruments and requires continued monitoring; we review detection and decontamination methods, and Euclid's contamination history. High-precision measurements of the zodiacal background reveal, at eight sigma significance, the subtle modulation caused by the changing perspective on the dust distribution due to the L2 halo-orbit libration. These data also show that conservative pre-launch estimates overestimated the out-of-field stray-light by factors of 4 (H band) to 27 (I band). Telemetry data demonstrate excellent guiding, and enable highly significant detections of solar radiation pressure and of thermal-emission recoil from Euclid's unilluminated dark sides. Lastly, we present a list of 34 meteoroid impacts, discuss their mechanical and optical signatures, and derive a minimum detectable impactor mass of 5e-7 g.

new.title: Direct estimation of the lunar-solar precession with geodetic very long baseline interferometry
new.summary: Geodetic very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) is capable of measuring the Earth's instantaneous rotation pole (IRP) components (hereafter, $X_{IRP}$ and $Y_{IRP}$) with sufficient accuracy using the VLBI delay rate. The least-squares fit of the $X_{IRP}$ and $Y_{IRP}$ polynomial expansion coefficients produces the precession model parameters independently of planetary motion theories. Our aim was to estimate the precession parameters using VLBI delay rate observations as well as the nutation coefficients in order to produce a full transformation matrix from the IRP to the Geocentric Celestial Reference System (GCRS). Then, the goal was to incorporate the free core nutation (FCN) effect from the VLBI group delay to form a complete and simple analytical model. We obtained an empirical model of the transformation from International Terrestrial Reference System (ITRS) to Geocentric Celestial Reference System (GCRS) based on observational results. Similar to the IAU2006 theory, the new model produces time series of $X_{IRP}$ and $Y_{IRP}$ angles, but these two angles now point out the direction of the IRP rather than the celestial intermediate pole (CIP). A simple analytical model defines the IRP location for any epoch during the interval of observations. Therefore, the non-rotation origin concept is not required for the transformation matrix construction. The estimate of the lunar-solar precessional parameter based on analysis of VLBI delay rate is $\psi_{A}= 5038.500\pm 0.019"$/cy (referred to the observational epoch 2000.0), which is close to the adopted IAU2006 precessional parameter value $\psi_{A}= 5038.4815 "$/cy.

new.title: Mitigating variance shrinkage in multi-task galaxy property inference from imaging data via statistical manifold alignment
new.summary: Inferring photometric redshifts ($z$) and key stellar population properties ($\log(M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot)$, $D_n4000$, and $\mathrm{H}\delta_A$) directly from multi-band imaging is increasingly critical for spectroscopically limited large surveys such as LSST and CSST. However, conventional point-wise loss functions (e.g., mean squared error or Huber loss) employed in deep neural networks often induce ``variance shrinkage''---a regression-to-the-mean effect that contracts predicted variances, distorts non-linear physical manifolds (such as bimodal distributions), and truncates heavy-tail populations. Here, we present ViTMultiTask, a vision transformer framework that incorporates a multi-scale maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss to enforce higher-order joint distribution alignment in reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Trained on 83,846 galaxies from Subaru HSC five-band ($g,r,i,z,y$) imaging cross-matched with DESI Data Release 1 Bright Galaxy Survey spectra, the model achieves high point-estimate precision on an independent test set of 5,000 galaxies: $\sigma_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.020$ for $z$, $0.169\,\mathrm{dex}$ for $\log(M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot)$, $0.073$ for $D_n4000$, and $1.185\,\text{Å}$ for $\mathrm{H}\delta_A$. Ablation experiments demonstrate that incorporating the MMD loss effectively mitigates variance shrinkage and more accurately reproduces the observed spectroscopic parameter distributions (including bimodal structures and heavy tails), while maintaining point-estimate accuracy statistically consistent with the baseline (RMSE changes $\le 3.5\%$) and catastrophic outlier rates fully comparable to the baseline. This kernel-based manifold alignment offers a statistically grounded and practical paradigm for comprehensive galaxy property inference in the deep imaging era.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) Euclid photometric masks
new.summary: This paper describes the Euclid DR1 photometric masks, which trace spatial variations in the survey properties (e.g. satellite position angles, integration time, sky tiling, and survey footprint); in the instrumental performance of Euclid and the external data (EXT) it uses (e.g. survey coverage, depth, PSF width, quality flags, systematic effects and astrometric uncertainties); and in possible contamination from sky emission (e.g. galactic extinction and zodiacal light emission). Among this, the effective coverage mask is particularly important as it defines the effective survey area and can be used to exclude spurious objects when selecting Euclid photometric samples for scientific analyses. The Euclid photometric masks are built for each observed sky region (tile) and are provided as full-sky HEALPix maps (nested ordering and explicit indexing) at Nside = 16 384, equating to a resolution of 12"88, for both the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Euclid Deep Survey (EDS). We estimate the total area of the DR1 EWS (EDS) to be 2008.8 (74.7) deg$^2$ and find that 82 (81)\% of this area is preserved by the effective coverage mask. We observe that Euclid's instrumental properties are consistent with expectations, showing only minor relative variations across the sky. For DR1 EWS the standard deviation of the depth (computed for a 2" aperture and at 5 $\sigma$) is below 0.2 AB mag, with median values of 25.69, 24.14, 24.3, and 24.29 for the Euclid IE, YE, JE, and HE bands. Finally, we expect these photometric masks to be key to many science applications and in particular for cosmological analyses.

new.title: Metadata for the Flux Density Calibration of the April 2021 and March 2022 Event Horizon Telescope Science Data
new.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has been conducting science observations annually since 2021 after the initial campaigns in 2017 and 2018. In this memo, we report on the metadata associated to the observations from 2021 April and 2022 March at 1.3mm wavelengths. We follow a similar path for the collection, processing, and validation of the metadata used for the initial amplitude calibration of the 2018 EHT data. In this release, we introduce some differences regarding the treatment of sensitivities and gain curves for some stations. In addition, we describe the changes to the EHT array since 2018.

new.title: Dissecting and diagnosing the LISA Galactic binary population
new.summary: LISA will individually resolve thousands of Galactic double white dwarf (DWD) binaries, while the majority stays buried in an unresolved gravitational wave (GW) confusion foreground. Which systems get resolved depends on the binary's parameters, on the global population and on instrumental sensitivity, so the resolved population is not a representative sample of the underlying Galactic population. Interpreting LISA's future catalog therefore requires understanding these selection effects. Here we characterize the resolved and unresolved subpopulations of a simulated Milky Way DWD catalog, using an iterative subtraction pipeline applied over different observation times. Resolvability is driven primarily by chirp mass: higher chirp mass, inspiraling systems are strongly favored over lower mass, outspiraling or monochromatic ones, and this reflects on the rate with which different composition subtypes are resolved. Spatially, resolved sources trace the Galactic bulge, because it is intrinsically the densest region of the Galaxy. The confusion background shows an internal bimodal chirp-mass structure, and is not generated uniformly by the same subpopulation in different frequency bands. We introduce a diagnostic for the minimum number of sources needed to reproduce a given fraction of the confusion power in a frequency band, and show that a residual confusion floor persists even after 100 years of integration. These biases are significant and need to be accounted for when using LISA's resolved DWD catalog and the confusion background to constrain the Galactic DWD population.

new.title: Kinessence, phantom crossing and sign-switching dark energy
new.summary: We introduce Kinessence models where combining K-mouflage and quintessence leads to phantom-crossing of the dark energy equation of state and sign-switching of the dark energy density. This is realised by joining a dark scalar sector comprising K-essence kinetic terms and a quintessence potential together with a Yukawa coupling to matter. We investigate the dynamics of these models in the Jordan frame at the background and perturbative levels. We concentrate on the effective equation of state and the matter fraction for the background. The CMB spectra, the linear power spectrum and the growth of structure via $f\sigma_8$ are also analysed at the perturbative level. The quintessence potential drives the acceleration of the Universe at low redshift with an equation of state greater than -1. The Yukawa coupling to matter leads to a phantom crossing behaviour depending on its strength. The potential fifth force mediated by the scalar field is screened by the K-mouflage mechanism triggered by the K-essence kinetic terms and passes Solar System tests. This allows for relatively large Yukawa couplings to matter $\beta\sim 0.1$, large enough to lead to the crossing of the phantom divide at $z\sim 0.5$. Despite a significant scalar interaction on large scales, we find that the growth of structure is reduced compared to LCDM. The matter fraction deviates from the standard model by a few percent and the Hubble rate is larger at low redshift than at recombination whilst the CMB spectra show small deviations from LCDM. The dark energy fraction becomes negative at redshifts greater than 2. All these features should alleviate the various tensions such as the larger value of $H_0$ at small redshift, a possible reduction of growth as measured by $S_8$ and the bound on the sum of the neutrino masses. Deviations from LCDM of the CMB lensing spectrum may provide a detectable window for these models.

new.title: Validating Updated Precession and Nutation Formulations for the Next IERS Conventions
new.summary: An international effort via the IAU/IAG Joint Working Group on Consistent Improvement of Earth's Rotation Theory (CIERT) aims to update the nutation theory to meet the milliarcsecond accuracy required by GGOS. While a companion article provides the theoretical background to the proposed precession-nutation corrections, this work presents their VLBI-based observational validation. The analysis systematically evaluates the revised models within practical application in VLBI analysis. These results provide critical empirical input for the upcoming integration of consistent, validated Earth rotation models into the next IERS Conventions.

new.title: Residual ellipticity driven by intense magnetic stress in the hot neutron star era
new.summary: A neutron star with a nonaxisymmetric mass distribution continuously radiates gravitational waves. The amplitude depends on the magnitude of the deformation, and is crucial for gravitational-wave astronomy. We studied an evolutionary effect on the magnetically induced ellipticity in the neutron star crust. A large deformation at the hot era before solidification is assumed to be produced magneto-hydrodynamically, and the fate at later time follows owing to the decrease in the force associated with the decay and redistribution of the current. Instead of simulating the evolution of deformation with the magnetic field over a long timescale, we estimate the ellipticity that remains after the formation of the solid crust by comparing two equilibrium models before and after solidification. The relic ellipticity is $\sim 10^{-8} (B_0/10^{13}{\rm{G}})^2$ in the magnitude for dipole field strength $B_{0}$ at the surface. This value was primarily determined by the magnetic field at the later time, with a weak dependence on the initial large deformation. The memory of the presolidification state was retained, but was small because the elastic force contributes little to the equilibrium.

new.title: Double Blandford: Resistive GRMHD simulations of accreting black holes simultaneously launch winds and jets
new.summary: Magnetic fields can launch outflows through the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) or the Blandford-Payne (BP) mechanism in accreting black hole systems. Despite the dominant launching mechanism still being unclear, the BP process has been insufficiently studied in general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations due to difficulties in generating and maintaining the required large-scale magnetic field geometry. Here, we set up six resistive GRMHD simulations of thin accretion disks with BHAC. The accretion disks in two simulations become magnetically arrested, while the others stay in the standard and normal evolution (SANE) regime. All simulations form jets and winds. The jets are parabolic and collimated by the outer sub-relativistic disk wind; a power law relating the jet width $x$ to the height $z$ as $x\propto z^\mathcal{K}$ yields exponents between 0.52 and 0.64. Among the SANE simulations, the setup with spin parameter $a_* = -0.9375$ has the strongest and most efficient jet, as it accumulates the most magnetic flux at the black hole horizon. For a highly spinning black hole with $a_*=0.9375$, the BZ jet power is $\gtrsim3$ times greater than the disk wind power. The simulated wind regions consist of a highly magnetized region, where the magnetization parameter $\sigma\gg1$, and a less magnetized region. A fast outflow with the potential to reach Lorentz factors up to $\Gamma_\infty\approx25$ propagates in the former region, but because the Lorentz force acts against the disk, it cannot remove a measurable amount of mass from the disk. In the less-magnetized region, a centrifugally driven slower wind efficiently carries away disk material.

new.title: Solar models using OPLIB monochromatic opacities
new.summary: Context. Opacity is a key ingredient in describing the transport of energy in stars. There are several methods for calculating stellar opacities, resulting in different tables (OPAL, OP, OPAS, and OPLIB). These opacities are available in two distinct forms: tables that regroup the Rosseland mean opacity pre-calculated at predefined chemical mixtures, and monochromatic opacity spectra of individual chemical elements, which allow for the computation of Rosseland mean opacity for a precise mixture. Aims. This study presents our implementation of the OPLIB monochromatic opacity data in Cesam2k20 and compares the solar-calibrated model obtained with these opacities to helioseismic data in order to evaluate the improvements made by using monochromatic opacities. Methods. We implemented the OPLIB monochromatic opacity data in the Cesam2k20 stellar evolution code following the method already used for the OP monochromatic opacity data. Results. We found that calibrated solar models produced with monochromatic opacity data (OP and OPLIB) agree better overall with helioseismic constraints than those produced with pre-calculated opacity tables.

new.title: Satellite pairs in the Local Group: from spatial clustering to dynamical associations in observations and $Λ$CDM simulations
new.summary: We investigate the incidence and physical nature of satellite galaxy pairs in the Local Group using updated observational data for the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31), together with analogues from the HESTIA constrained cosmological simulations. Our comparison uses three distinct simulated Local Group analogues drawn from the HESTIA suite, allowing us to assess the observed pair statistics against multiple cosmological realisations of the Local Group environment. We identify close nearest-neighbour associations by comparing the observed satellite distributions with isotropic populations that reproduce the radial distributions of each host, and investigate their physical nature using line-of-sight velocities, proper motions, and gravitational binding estimates. We find that the MW exhibits a significant excess of close satellite associations relative to isotropic expectations, with a pairing efficiency of $\sim53\%$, nearly twice that found in the simulated analogues ($\sim17$-$27\%$). This excess persists after applying a stellar mass cut ($M_\star > 10^4\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) to match the resolution limits of the simulations. In contrast, the M31 satellite system is broadly consistent with isotropy, with a pairing efficiency of $\sim28\%$. However, only a minority of pair candidates exhibit coherent kinematics or are likely to be gravitationally bound, indicating that most represent transient alignments or remnants of common group infall rather than long-lived binary satellites. These results suggest that the MW hosts an unusually rich population of phase-space-correlated satellites, likely reflecting its recent accretion history, whereas M31 is more consistent with typical $\Lambda$CDM expectations.

new.title: Efficient Standard Siren Cosmological Inference with Posterior Reuse
new.summary: Standard siren cosmology depends on several modelling assumptions, including the underlying source population, galaxy catalogue, and detection selection function. Quantifying the effect of each choice typically requires a full, independent analysis. As gravitational-wave catalogs grow incrementally, much computational effort is spent re-analysing largely overlapping datasets. We apply the recently developed ASPIRE (Accelerated Sequential Posterior Inference via Reuse) sampler to the joint estimation of cosmological and population parameters with dark sirens. ASPIRE updates existing posterior samples into the posterior under a new hypothesis without restarting from the prior. It combines normalising flows with a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) scheme to produce accurate posteriors and unbiased evidence estimates. Applying ASPIRE to a number of dark siren analysis cases with GWTC-5.0, we recover posteriors consistent with nested sampling, while recording a performance improvement of between 6-28 times over the set of analyses when using an existing posterior. This enables efficient exploration of modelling choices and rapid updates as catalogs grow, without duplicating existing computational effort.

new.title: Active Learning for Molecular Discovery: A Retrospective Test toward TMC-1
new.summary: Machine-learning recommendation lists can help prioritize searches for new interstellar molecules, but whether reranking such a list as detections accumulate improves on it has not been tested. We present a pre-registered retrospective test toward TMC-1, using a published machine-learning list of 1,510 recommended candidates, consolidated to 1,434 candidates, and the species reported there through September 2026. At four annual origins from 2022 to 2025, a logistic-regression ranking on seven released features, refit on the detections known at each origin, separates later detections from never-detected candidates with a pooled AUC of 0.867, against 0.706 for the best single-criterion baseline (difference 0.160; 95\% interval 0.095-0.230). The advantage persists under a shifted date boundary and two alternative feature regimes, but is not established among the top 100 candidates (12 versus 7 detections). A searcher that refits on its own observations reaches half of the 63 detected species on the list in a median of 200 observations, against 332 for the best fixed ordering and 717.5 expected for random search. Uncertainty sampling, the standard active-learning rule, performs worse than random (AUC 0.210): later detections lie at low predictive uncertainty, close to known chemistry. Of 101 species in our validation set, 37 are absent from the list, and only 13 of these appear in a pool rebuilt from its source databases, including 2 of 11 radicals and neither ion. Candidate generation, not ranking, is the main constraint. We release 100 recommended targets, with code and frozen inputs, for prospective testing.

new.title: Global climate modeling of the Martian water cycle. I) Improved parameterizations of physical processes
new.summary: We implement four new physical parameterizations relevant to the water cycle in the Mars PCM (previously Mars Laboratoire de M{é}t{é}orologie Dynamique GCM)\,: the latent heat of ground ice sublimation, a temperature-dependent nucleation scheme in cloud microphysics, differentiated albedos for water frost and perennial ice and scavenging of water ice clouds by CO2 particle formation. After a new tuning of the poorly known model parameters, we find that combining these parameterizations allows for an improved agreement of the modeled water cycle compared to Thermal Emission Spectrometer column-integrated vapor and ice retrievals. We show that latent heat cooling prevents the formation of surface liquid water at present and likely in the recent past on Mars. Using two albedos corrects the overestimation of the northern sublimation event, a major defect of the model. Our study highlights that each parameterization has indirect consequences amplified by the radiatively active clouds. We stress that the increasingly complex water cycle in the Mars PCM should be studied in the future using numerical methods tailored for climate modeling, in addition to the effect of each individual component.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Persistence in NISP detectors
new.summary: Detector persistence is a significant source of systematic error in infrared observations and affects the scientific performance of the \Euclid Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP). We characterise persistence using complementary ground calibration and in-flight data, develop empirical models of its temporal evolution, and assess its impact on science observations and the \Euclid data-processing pipeline. Persistence is highly non-uniform across the focal plane, with variations of up to two orders of magnitude between and within detectors. Its amplitude is typically below 1\% of the stimulus signal and depends nonlinearly on the preceding fluence. The decay rate is faster for brighter sources. During mission operations, the persistence signal has progressively decreased by roughly 10\%, while the decay rate has remained approximately stable. Persistence following over-saturating signals does not follow the empirical relations derived for under-saturating fluences and plausibly reduces persistence response over longer timescales. The impact of charge trapping and release on flat-field observations and on the background in science exposures is also discussed. Persistence measured in science observations is observed to differ systematically from that derived from dark calibration data. In addition, persistence of energetic particle hits is observed to be different from that of astronomical sources of comparable signal. Finally, we discuss the impact of persistence on \Euclid NISP observations and describe the masking strategy adopted for the Q1 abd DR1 releases, focusing on identifying which pixels are affected by persistence and for how long they should be excluded from science observations.

new.title: Inertial modes in a turbulent rotating magneto-convection simulation with the solar-like differential rotation
new.summary: Recent observations have revealed a variety of solar inertial modes, but their nonlinear properties remain largely unexplored. We aim to identify and characterize inertial modes in a state-of-the-art simulation of rotating magnetoconvection, in which solar-like differential rotation was self-consistently reproduced. We analyzed nine years of high-cadence data from the Hotta (2025) simulation. The spatial eigenfunctions of various low-frequency inertial modes were extracted using singular value decomposition. We identified major classes of retrograde inertial modes, including equatorial Rossby modes, high-latitude modes, and high-frequency retrograde modes, with frequencies and near-surface amplitudes roughly consistent with the solar observations. In particular, thanks to the strongly baroclinic background in the simulation, the observed large amplitude ($\sim 10$ m/s) and the characteristic polar spiral pattern of the high-latitude mode at azimuthal order $m=1$ are successfully reproduced. This indicates that high-latitude modes are excited by baroclinic instability, which can occur even amid turbulent convection. We further show that the prograde columnar modes undergo a qualitative transition at $m \sim 6$, separating the fast-propagating convective modes at $m \gtrsim 6$ from thermally diffusive slow modes at $m \lesssim 6$ whose frequencies closely match recent observational inferences of thermal Rossby modes. Finally, we find that turbulent magnetic fields primarily influence the inertial modes indirectly through modifications of the background state. Our results suggest that the observed properties of solar inertial modes are broadly consistent with a simulation in which solar-like differential rotation is maintained in a magnetically dominated regime, although the simulation still overproduces prograde columnar modes at large $m$.

new.title: Combining TTVs, RVs, and astrometry to characterize distant giant companions of transiting hot Jupiters: Application to WASP-4
new.summary: The origins and architectures of hot Jupiter (HJ) systems remain unclear, with potential explanations for the tight orbits being in-situ formation, disk-migration, or high-eccentricity migration. These mechanisms can leave different imprints on the orbital architecture, but tidal interactions act to erase these imprints for HJs, leading to orbital circularization, realignment, and potentially orbital decay. The latter can be mimicked by the introduction of light travel-time effects (LTTE) caused by an outer giant companion, as for WASP-4$\,$b. We examine the WASP-4 system using newly obtained ESO$\,$3.6/HARPS radial velocity (RV) observations and archival transit-timing data, leveraging the LTTE. Furthermore, we present a novel approach of analyzing HJ systems in sight of $\textit{Gaia}$'s Data Release 4. We propose combining RV, transit-timing, and astrometry data, making use of the LTTE as a proxy for the orbital motion of a possible outer companion. We combine and fit all currently available data and simulate $\textit{Gaia}$ DR4 and DR5 astrometric measurements of WASP-4 and perform an injection and recovery procedure to estimate their impact on the recovered planetary parameters of WASP-4$\,$c. The procedure employs a combined model that describes RVs, transit timing variations (TTVs) via the LTTE, and astrometry simultaneously. Analyzing the existing data, we improve the planetary parameters of WASP-4$\,$c, finding a minimum mass of $9.3\pm1.7\,M_\mathrm{Jup}$ with an orbital period of $10\,600^{+1100}_{-1000}\,$d, or about $29\,$yr. Furthermore, we find that there is no significant orbital decay taking place for WASP-4$\,$b. In simulations of $\textit{Gaia}$ DR5, our three-pronged approach reduces the error bars of WASP-4$\,$c's parameters by about $10\%$, $25\%$, and $33\%$ for its orbital period, time of inferior conjunction, and RV semi-amplitude, respectively. new.title: The Same But Different: SiO$_2$ Clouds in Two L-Dwarfs with JWST
new.summary: The precision of brown dwarf spectra from JWST enables unprecedented insight into the atmospheric and cloud properties of sub-stellar atmospheres. Here, we compare both self-consistent radiative-convective equilibrium (RCE) and retrieval atmosphere models to high-SNR 1--18~$\mu$m spectra of two field L-dwarfs from JWST, J0624 (L5) and J2148 (L6--L6.5). Our observations include spectral features from H$_2$O, CO, CO$_2$, CH$_4$, Na, and K and cover approximately 98\% of the outgoing thermal emission from the two objects. We first compare the data to three independent grids of 1D-RCE models: BT-Settl, exoREM, and Sonora Diamondback. While exoREM provides the best fit of the grid models, no 1D-RCE model provides a satisfactory fit to the data, highlighting the complexity of fitting cloudy L-dwarf spectra. Nonetheless, the temperature and cloud properties can be constrained with the 1D-RCE models, while metallicity, C/O ratio, and surface gravity are not well-measured. Next, we use petitRADTRANS to retrieve atmosphere and cloud properties, finding strong evidence for the presence of SiO$_2$ clouds in both objects. The SiO$_2$ is found to be amorphous in structure for J0624 but crystalline in J2148, highlighting important differences in objects of similar spectral type. We also used a non-Bayesian optimization framework to explore a wider variety of cloud scenarios, finding evidence for the inclusion of iron-rich magnesium silicates (Mg$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$SiO$_3$, MgFeSiO$_4$) in addition to SiO$_2$ in both objects. These results show both the complexity and diversity of brown dwarf cloud properties, while also highlighting the constraining power of broad-wavelength JWST observations of cloudy L-dwarfs.

new.title: Bayesian Inference of Fermionic Dark Matter Admixed Neutron Stars Informed by Galaxy Cluster Constraints
new.summary: Self-interacting dark matter is constrained on galactic and cluster scales by its elastic scattering cross section per unit mass, $\sigma/m_\chi \sim 0.1-10\ {\rm cm^2/g}$. We incorporate this cross section into the equation of state of an asymmetric, self-interacting fermionic dark matter component and perform a Bayesian inference of dark matter admixed neutron stars in the two-fluid framework at $\sigma/m_\chi = 0.1$, $1$ and $10\ {\rm cm^2/g}$. Seven nuclear matter parameters are sampled together with the dark particle mass and mass fraction, and confronted with nuclear theory and neutron star observations. The nuclear sector and the global observables are statistically indistinguishable across the whole range of cross sections, while the data constrain the dark matter mass to $m_\chi \simeq 1.45-1.88$~GeV and its mass fraction to $f_\chi \simeq 0.05-0.09$, depending on the cross section. Finally, comparing runs built from the same parameter draws, so that only the cross section differs, we find that it does change the baryonic radius appreciably, but only for light dark matter, a region the astrophysical data largely disfavor. The self-interaction is therefore not too weak to be seen; however its effect is hidden in the region of parameter space that the present observational data already disfavor.

new.title: Radiative Transfer Modeling of Multi-Shell Molecular Outflows in the Class 0 Protostar IRAS 15398-3359
new.summary: Recent high-angular-resolution observations of protostellar outflows have revealed complex spatial and velocity structures that are difficult to describe with a single shell. We have investigated the primary outflow of the Class 0 protostar IRAS 15398$-$3359 in the H$_2$CO and CS emission observed with ALMA and identified four shell-like components, which trace the cavity walls of the more extended CO outflows. Non-LTE radiative-transfer calculations of H$_2$CO and synthetic ALMA observations of the three-dimensional model show that a common ellipsoidal geometrical form and Hubble-law-like velocity field can broadly reproduce the channel-map and position--velocity structures of the identified shells when the geometry, spatial configuration, and kinematics of each shell are allowed to vary independently. The kinematic timescales and inclination angles of the inner and outer shells are $\sim$1000 yr ($19^\circ$ and $15^\circ$) and $\sim$750 yr ($5^\circ$ and $8^\circ$), respectively. The momentum injection rate of the outer bipolar pair is approximately 2.2 times that of the inner pair. The inferred $\dot{M}_{\rm wind}/\dot{M}_{\rm acc}$ ratios are $0.7$--$3\%$ and $2$--$7\%$ for the inner and outer shells. The observed shell-to-shell differences suggest episodicity of the mass ejection events, where the strength and direction of the outflow activity may vary over short timescales of order $10^2$--$10^3$ yr.

new.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Multi-band photometry validation on COSMOS extragalactic sources
new.summary: The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) contains catalogues of sources covering 1900 deg2, including deep coverage of legacy fields that enable an extensive comparison between Euclid imaging and multiwavelength observations from other instruments. The Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field, observed by Euclid and included in DR1, has been observed with the James Webb Space Telescope, resulting in the COSMOS2025 catalogue. We compare the Euclid DR1 photometry with the multiwavelength COSMOS2025 data to assess the accuracy of the photometric measurements produced by the different methods implemented in the OU-MER pipeline. We use both the Euclid Wide and Deep Surveys, focussing exclusively on extragalactic sources. We use the fluxes of COSMOS2025 to predict the expected fluxes in the Euclid bands via spectral energy distribution fitting, while the redshifts are either spectroscopic, for a sample of brighter sources, or photometric, to include fainter sources. Both the fluxes in the common Hyper Suprime-Cam bands and the SEDs from COSMOS2025 are used to validate the analysis and to characterise any biases or limitations of the method. The predicted fluxes and the OU-MER measurements are in good agreement, especially for bright and isolated sources. Median offsets depend on band, photometric method, survey depth, and redshift sample, most well within 10%, the largest offset seen in the NIR bands for the deep photo-z model-fitting measurements. However, complementary measurements on Gaia stars show an opposite trend, highlighting that photometric validation approaches may suffer from intrinsic uncertainties that prevent a thorough assessment of systematic effects. Among the three methods, template-fitting photometry generally shows the smallest offset from the SED-based predictions in the NISP bands and toward fainter magnitudes, while aperture photometry and model-fitting are comparable in IE.

new.title: Magellanic Outflow and Chemistry Survey (MAGOS): the Outflow-Luminosity Scaling Relations in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds
new.summary: Understanding massive star formation in low-metallicity environments is crucial for constraining the universality of star formation across cosmic evolution. In this Letter, we present the first systematic survey of massive protostellar outflows in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC, $Z\sim$0.2--0.5 $Z_\odot$), as part of the Magellanic Outflow and Chemistry Survey (MAGOS). MAGOS targets 40 massive young stellar objects (MYSOs) with luminosities of (1--23)$\times 10^4$ $L_\odot$ with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 0.85 mm at a linear resolution of $\sim$0.1 pc. Using CO (3--2), we identify blue- and red-shifted outflows associated with the primary continuum sources toward 29 targets in the LMC and 10 targets in the SMC. Comparing the outflow mass, momentum, energy, and force versus luminosity scaling relations in MAGOS with those in the Galaxy, we find that the LMC CO outflows have a similar slope in the mass-luminosity relation, suggesting that CO remains an effective tracer of massive protostellar outflows at $Z\sim$0.5 $Z_\odot$. In contrast, despite the large scatter, the SMC CO outflows are deficient at high luminosity and show flatter scaling relations than the LMC and the Galaxy. This is consistent with reduced CO abundances due to enhanced photodissociation at high luminosity and low metallicity ($Z\sim$0.2 $Z_\odot$), although the possibility of intrinsically weak outflow launching cannot be ruled out with the current data.

new.title: The $w$-mode instability of strangeon ergostars and its impact on energy extraction
new.summary: Rapidly rotating compact ergostars have been proposed as alternative central engines for short gamma-ray bursts. However, competing energy-loss channels, such as gravitational-wave emission driven by non-axisymmetric instabilities, could curtail the power available for relativistic electromagnetic outflows. In this work, we investigate the $w$-mode instability of rapidly rotating strangeon ergostars by solving the coupled spacetime and fluid perturbation equations in the Hilbert gauge using a spectral method, without relying on a slow-rotation approximation. We calculate the complex eigenvalues of the axial-led and polar-led $w$-mode branches originating from the fundamental $l=m=2$ modes of nonrotating stars along the maximum-energy-extraction paths of twelve representative strangeon equations of state. We find that both branches remain damped throughout these paths, despite the presence of ergoregions. We further vary the stellar angular velocity to determine the instability thresholds. In every case with an identified threshold, the angular velocity at the corresponding extraction-path endpoint remains below the critical value, with the largest ratio being $0.926$. Our results indicate that the $w$-mode instabilities examined here do not provide a growing gravitational-wave emission channel along the considered energy-extraction paths, supporting the availability of the previously estimated rotational energy reservoirs for electromagnetic extraction.

new.title: A parametrized simulation code to simulate the response of ground detector arrays to Extensive Air Showers above 100 TeV
new.summary: Surface arrays detecting the secondary particles of Extensive Air Showers (EAS) are one of the techniques used to detect gamma-rays from high-energy sources. To evaluate the reconstruction performance, gamma/hadron separation, and sensitivity of such experiments, many simulations of gamma rays and protons are required. The usual approach is divided into two steps. First, the CORSIKA software is used to generate EAS at the observation level. Then, a GEANT4-based full simulation code is used to simulate the array response. For very large fill factors, above 30-100 TeV, the computational resources required become too demanding. In this work, the authors present an alternative way to evaluate the performance-related quantities of a simulated array configuration through the parametrization of the detector response. We will present the implementation of such software, the validation checks we performed, and the application of this tool to a representative future ground-based water-Cherenkov detector array.

new.title: Lense-Thirring induced repeating blast trains in continuous gravitational waves
new.summary: We characterise gravitational lensing induced by the Lense-Thirring effect in a continuous gravitational-wave source orbiting a spinning supermassive black hole. This scenario is very likely to generate lensing events, as long as the source's orbital inclination is not aligned with the black hole's spin axis and the Lense-Thirring timescale is shorter than the observational window. The signal appears as short-duration ($T_{\rm blast}$) gravitational-wave "blasts" that repeat after every orbit ($T_{\rm orb}$) within a limited time window ($T_{\rm train}$). The blasts' signal strength depends on the system's geometry and not on the black hole mass. The signal will go silent and renew twice in a full Lense-Thirring precession period.

new.title: Localization of gravitational-wave source behind galaxy clusters by gravitational-wave lensing
new.summary: Gravitational-wave observations have opened new opportunities to study massive object events like merging binary black holes. When combined with electromagnetic counterparts, accurate localization of gravitational-wave sources could allow us to identify their host galaxies and carry out follow-up studies, such as study the environment of merging black holes and determine the Hubble constant. One of the possible methods for precise localization is strong gravitational-wave lensing. Previous studies have considered strong gravitational-wave lensing with galaxy lenses. However, galaxy clusters have yet to be investigated due to the complexity of their mass structures. Here we take the list of known cluster lenses from the Hubble Frontier Fields, simulate lensing properties of gravitational waves from their reconstructions as they would be observed by the ground-based gravitational-wave detectors. When same model family is used in simulation and localization, we find that the correct lens is identified for around 90\% of the simulated events. We also show that the source positions within the cluster can be pinpointed at sub-arcsecond precision with an estimate on source redshift. When we marginalize over all possible lens models for the clusters, the lens identification and localizations remain valid as long as the correct lens model is contained in the available cluster lens models. However, most localization attempts fail at initialization if the correct cluster model is excluded. These tests establish a proof of concept of localization under idealized conditions, while more work is needed to understand the cluster lens modeling discrepancies and reconstruction bias to validate the approach further.
